title: Dropping Just a Handful of Preferences Can Change Top Large Language Model Rankings
claim: Removing a tiny subset of the data can flip the top-ranked item in a leaderboard.
layout: 3 regions, left-to-right, magnifier zooms dropped subset into ranking flip
description: A cartoon in three regions read left to right. On the left, a large orange circle labeled 'Full Arena' stands for the whole preference dataset. A tiny orange dot is cut from it and shown under a magnifying glass labeled 'Dropped Subset'. A dashed line leads from the lens to a rounded box showing one example preference: the prompt 'write a haiku about rain' with model a and model b responses drawn as dashes. On the right, two stacked rounded boxes list leaderboard rankings. The top box shows #1 Gemini-1.5-pro, #2 GPT-4o in red, and #3 Claude-3-5-sonnet. A thick black arrow points down to the bottom box, where GPT-4o in red is now #1 and Gemini-1.5-pro is #2. The orange circle and the red text draw the eye first.
caption: Our method (i) tests whether AI leaderboard rankings remain stable upon dropping small fractions of data and (ii) pinpoints the specific data points (e.g., preferences) that drive ranking flips.
abstract: We propose a method for evaluating the robustness of widely used LLM ranking systems -- variants of a Bradley--Terry model -- to dropping a worst-case very small fraction of preference data. Our approach is computationally fast and easy to adopt. When we apply our method to matchups from popular LLM ranking platforms, including Chatbot Arena and derivatives, we find that the rankings of top-performing models can be remarkably sensitive to the removal of a small fraction of preferences; for instance, dropping just 0.003% of human preferences can change the top-ranked model on Chatbot Arena. Our robustness check identifies the specific preferences most responsible for such ranking flips, allowing for inspection of these influential preferences. We observe that the rankings derived from MT-bench preferences are notably more robust than those from Chatbot Arena, likely due to MT-bench's use of expert annotators and carefully constructed prompts. Finally, we find that neither rankings based on crowdsourced human evaluations nor those based on LLM-as-a-judge preferences are systematically more sensitive than the other.
